hook: Donald Hebb trained first in English literature at Dalhousie University before turning to psychology, earning a master's degree at McGill University and then a PhD at Harvard under Karl Lashley, whose research on the brain's role in learning shaped Hebb's own direction. After periods at Queen's University and the Yerkes Laboratories of Primate Biology, he joined McGill University in 1947, where he spent the rest of his career and eventually chaired the psychology department. In 1949 he published The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory, proposing that learning and memory arise physically in the brain when one neuron's repeated activity helps fire another, strengthening the connection between them, a mechanism now known as Hebbian learning or Hebb's postulate. That idea gave later researchers a concrete, biologically grounded rule for how neural connections might change with experience, and it became a founding principle for artificial neural network models, from Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron through much later connectionist research. Hebb also developed the Hebb-Williams maze for testing animal intelligence and studied how early experience and sensory deprivation shape later behavior. He remained closely tied to McGill until his death in 1985, having also served as the university's chancellor.
name: Donald Hebb

quote.text: When an axon of cell A is near enough to excite a cell B and repeatedly or persistently takes part in firing it, some growth process or metabolic change takes place in one or both cells such that A's efficiency, as one of the cells firing B, is increased.
quote.context: The Organization of Behavior: A Neuropsychological Theory, 1949

quick_facts: Proposed the Hebbian learning rule in his 1949 book The Organization of Behavior
Earned his PhD in psychology at Harvard University under Karl Lashley
Spent most of his career at McGill University, later serving as its chancellor
Developed the Hebb-Williams maze for testing animal problem-solving ability
His theory of neurons that strengthen connections through repeated joint activity became a founding principle of artificial neural network research

achievements.title: The Organization of Behavior, 1949
achievements.impact: Proposed that learning occurs through strengthened connections between neurons that fire together, giving neuroscience and later artificial intelligence a concrete rule for how experience can change a network.

achievements.title: Hebbian learning rule (Hebb's postulate)
achievements.impact: Became a foundational principle for artificial neural network research, directly influencing later weight-update rules used in perceptrons and connectionist models.

achievements.title: Hebb-Williams maze
achievements.impact: Developed a standardized maze test for measuring problem-solving ability in animals, widely used in comparative psychology.

achievements.title: Research on early experience and sensory deprivation
achievements.impact: Showed that early sensory and environmental experience shapes later intelligence and behavior, influencing developmental psychology.
